titulo.texto: Frieze of the Jaguars and Coyotes

frase_gancho.texto: Beasts of stone on parade, and eagles that devour hearts.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the coyotes of the frieze, we move to a single one, and to a man emerging from its jaws: a warrior who dressed as an animal to resemble it.

guion_corto.texto: This slab belongs to the friezes of Pyramid B at Tula and preserves traces of red, blue, and white. In one band, pumas, jaguars, and coyotes walk in procession, with necklaces around their necks. In another, royal eagles and vultures hold human hearts between their beaks and talons. These are not mere decorations: they are thought to be the emblems of the warrior orders of Tula, each of which had an animal as its symbol. War, for them, had a sacred mission: to capture prisoners and feed the Sun with hearts, so that the world could go on. It is a harsh image, but an orderly one: animals marching in line, like an army.

guion_largo.texto:
Imagine the facade of Pyramid B as a page of stone. In each horizontal band, a scene repeats: whoever crossed the plaza did not need to know how to read, because the pyramid told them what mattered. This slab is a fragment of that book, and today it lets you read one complete page.

Start with the lower band, or the upper one, the band of the walkers. Pumas, jaguars, and coyotes advance with their mouths open, their tongues out, and bead necklaces around their necks. These are not wild animals: they wear jewels. And they all advance in the same direction, with the rhythm of a procession. An animal that walks like this is an animal with a rank, just like a soldier in uniform.

Now look at the other scene. A royal eagle and a king vulture, the bird with the colorful head that appears in many codices, hold a human heart between their beaks and talons. The heart, yollotl in Nahuatl, was the food of the Sun. The Toltecs believed, as the Mexica would later, that if the Sun did not receive its nourishment, it would stop moving. War thus had a practical purpose: to capture prisoners to offer them to the sky.

Where have you seen these animals before? In Teotihuacán, coyotes paraded, painted on the walls of Atetelco; in Tequixquiac, the coyote appears, perhaps for the first time, carved in bone. Here they become official emblems. It is as if the coyote had risen in rank over the millennia: from an animal of the prairie to the military symbol of a capital.

It is thought that the Toltecs organized their warriors into orders, each with its own animal. The Mexica would later have the orders of the Eagle and the Jaguar, and would present them as heirs to that tradition. We know more about the Mexica orders, because chroniclers described them, than about the Toltec ones, which we know mostly through images like this one. That is why it is better to say “it is thought,” and not “it is known.”

There is another connection that will surprise you. According to the legend of the founding of Tenochtitlan, the eagle was to perch on a prickly pear cactus, and it was said that this cactus had grown from the heart of Copil, an enemy of the Mexica. The red prickly pears of the cactus were, then, hearts. The eagle on the National Coat of Arms that you saw on the facade of the museum is a distant cousin of these eagles of Tula, which also eat hearts.

If you step closer to the stone, you will notice that the animals are separated by bands and that the colors, though worn, keep their strength. The slab reminds us that Tula was not a place of gray ruins, but a painted city, noisy and full of symbols. And when the city burned, around the year eleven fifty, these slabs fell and were covered in ash, safe from the centuries.

The frieze, finally, is a form of propaganda: it showed the people who the defenders of the world were and what the price of keeping order was. It is an art that does not ask permission: it commands.

texto: Count how many different animals parade along the band
Find the heart the eagle holds between its beak and talons
Look closely at the necklaces of the felines and the coyotes

texto.Material: Volcanic rock slabs carved in relief, with traces of mineral pigments

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Mexica invented the idea of the eagle and jaguar warriors.
texto.respuesta: Reality: These images were already at Tula, centuries earlier; the Mexica presented themselves as heirs to that tradition.
